en: The Mahāmāyā Tantra, together with the commentary by Guṇavatī; the first instruction.
Homage to the glorious Vajraḍākinīs!
Homage to the glorious Vajraḍākinī, the sovereign of the circle of ḍākinīs, who possesses the five wisdoms and the three bodies, and who provides protection for the world. (1)
Homage to the virtuous Śrī Bhūtaḍāmara,
by whom bodies were fashioned for the sake of the welfare of the world.
The families, the goddesses, and the lords of the families—
seek that Vajradhara, who has realized the single reality following the mudrās of their forms, for the sake of auspiciousness.
The *Mahāmāyātantra* is exceedingly light in its words yet profound in its meaning;
in this world, there are now only a few who know it without interruption.
Therefore, for those who possess pure knowledge and are adorned with sacred learning, [the commentary] exists at every step therein.
This exertion of mine is intended to make that which is difficult to attain in the world easily accessible.
The Sugata has taught various paths to enlightenment, having observed that the world has diverse inclinations;
many have been personally engaged according to their own preferences.
My exposition here is endowed with virtue, as is my action.
And those Vajra-Ḍākinīs, having severed the bonds of conceptual construction, have entered into worldly activities and take delight therein. ||2||
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the most secret *tantra* named *Vajraḍākinīguhyeśvarī*. 3.
"Then," and so forth. This tantra is not independent (*muktaka*). What then? It is joined with other tantras.
Therefore, this word "then" (*atha*) indicates the immediate succession of this tantra in relation to a preceding tantra.
It washes away [impurity]. For this very reason, the introductory statement beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā*) and so forth was employed at the beginning of this [work],
because it has already been employed previously,
as in the *Śrīvajraśekhara*.

"From this" (ataḥ): because this alone is the swift means for awakening for those who delight in extreme brevity, therefore [the author] says "I shall explain"—this is the connection. "I shall explain" (pravakṣye) means I shall explain by dividing [the subject matter].
"Tantra" means a continuous composition (*prabandha*).
Tantra is threefold: the tantra of cause (*hetu-tantra*), the tantra of result (*phala-tantra*), and [the tantra of means].
And there is the Method Tantra (*upāyatantra*).
In that context, the mind that is naturally luminous and without beginning or end is the *bodhicitta*; its seed, together with its cause, is that [same] mind.
Of what is it the seed? Of awakening.
Perfectly complete awakening is the fruit, because it is the unsurpassed fruit.
Furthermore, that is the purification characterized by the exhaustion of all adventitious obscurations of that very mind which is naturally luminous.
It is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas;
the meaning is that it is the basis for the infinite Buddha-qualities comprised within the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
That very awakening of the Buddhas is the Dharmakāya, the state of the Great Vajradhara.
For that reason, the means for the complete accomplishment of that fruit is the *sādhana*.
Furthermore, that is the path of the Bodhisattvas, cultivated over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*), together with its auxiliary practices.

In this Mantrayāna, there is a path consisting of the maṇḍala-cakra and its associated equipment, which is a condensed form of that very same great path to enlightenment; it is a means for achieving enlightenment more swiftly and more easily.
With reference to these causes, fruits, and means, there are hundreds of scriptural treatises of instruction, which are respectively termed *hetu-tantra*, *phala-tantra*, or *upāya-tantra*.
I shall now proclaim this threefold tantra.

To the question "What, then, is the name of that tantra?", he says: "Its name is 'Supremely Secret' (Paramagupta). The indeclinable word *nāma* is used here in the sense of well-known renown (*prasiddhi*). It is supremely secret.
The meaning is that it is well-known by this name.
To whom is it supremely secret?
He says: to the Vajra-Ḍākinīs.
And for this reason, this tantra is called *Vajraḍākinīparamaguhyam* in its entirety; however, by the elision of the first member of the compound, it is called *Paramaguhyam*,
just as *Satyabhāmā* is called *Bhāmā*.
In the root *ḍai* (meaning "to move through the air," class 1, no. 968), there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *e*.
Thus, from *ḍān*, we derive *ḍāḥ*, which means "moving through the sky."
The third case ending [is used] after the word *ḍā*. The root *aka* (and *aga*) is listed as meaning "to move in a crooked way" (Dhātupāṭha 792–793, bhvādi).
In this context, "crooked movement" refers to moving in all directions.
A *ḍākinī* is so called because her nature (*śila*) is to go (*kitum*); for she goes simultaneously in all directions across hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of points of space.
And thus it has been said:
"The root *ḍai* is here conceived in the sense of moving through the air;
thus she is renowned as the *ḍākinī*, the accomplishment of all forms of movement."
The mention of "vajra" is for the purpose of excluding external ḍākinīs;
"vajra" means the thunderbolt, because it consists of non-conceptual wisdom (*aprapañca-jñāna*).
"And the ḍākinīs" refers to the Vajra-ḍākinīs. To the question "Of what kind are they?", he says: "Of the mistresses of the secret.
Here, the five families are the five secrets.
Their sovereigns are the agents of creation and destruction.
Among them, the sovereign of the Tathāgata family is she by whom this entire cosmic egg, including all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded.
The origin of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, who possess great supernatural power.
Buddha-Ḍākinī,
Vajra-Ḍākinī of the Vajra family, and Ratna-Ḍākinī of the Maṇi family.
Padmaḍākinī is the mistress of the Pa family; Viśvaḍākinī is the mistress of the Ka family;
and Mahāmāyā is the mistress of them all as well.
Because she is the secret among those secrets that are exceedingly secret, she is therefore the supreme secret;
the tantra that expresses her is likewise so called.
For example, the poem titled *Sītāharaṇa*.
To demonstrate the meaning of this very name, he says "yayā" and so forth.
[The root] *bṛh* / *bṛhi* means "to grow" (*bhvādi*, 735–736); [the suffix] *manin* is applied.
There is a phonetic modification (*varṇavikāra*) according to etymological rules (*nairukta*).
Thus, it is "Brahmā.
However, here, because they are the gurus of all worlds, the Tathāgatas—who are the most venerable in every respect—are the "Brahmās," being comprised within the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies.
Their *aṇḍa* is the place of origin.
The meaning is the *dharmakāya*.

Alternatively, because it is the excellence of liberation, it is *brahmā*; and because it is the place of origin for those two bodies (*kāyadvaya*), it is the "egg" (*aṇḍa*); thus, *brahmāṇḍa* means the *dharmakāya*.
[Furthermore,] it refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) within the completely pure Buddha-fields.
That which is the receptacle world among them is "moving" here; that which is the sentient world among them is "non-moving" here.
That which exists together with those two is the "mobile and immobile" universe (sacarācara-brahmāṇḍa). The connection is that [the Lord] pervades that;
"entire" (sakala) means everything.
The meaning is "belonging to all Tathāgatas.
In that regard, how is the Brahmāṇḍa pervaded by her?
Because the Brahmāṇḍa of all Buddhas is composed of nothing but that.
Why are the worlds of the moving and the non-moving pervaded by her? Because they originate from her.
He states this very point with the words beginning "origination" (utpatti).
The cause is origination.
"Of all the gods" refers to the five *kula-ḍākinīs*; "of Brahmā and the others" refers to the five Tathāgatas;
and furthermore, it refers to each of the infinite families (*kulas*).
"Maharddhika" means one who possesses great power. ||4||
Among them, O Maheśvarī, this Mahāmāyā is the supreme secret;
Mahāmāyā is the great Raudrī, the cause of the destruction of all beings. ||5||
To the question "Who is this?", he says: "Mahāmāyā. By the term Mahāmāyā, the Lord Heruka—the most secret form of the Blessed One Vajradhara—is expressed.
Regarding the term *maheśvarī*: for Brahmā and the others are the creators of the gods; therefore, they possess great sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
They too were created by her;
therefore, she is Maheśvarī. Since she is Maheśvarī, [she is so called].
For this very reason, this is their supreme secret.
"Of them" refers to the Vajra-Ḍākinīs.
"Supreme secret" means the most secret.
"This" refers to Mahāmāyā. For it is said that she is the secret of both subtle and gross forms; consequently, the five lords of the families (kulādhipas) of the five families are the five secrets.

The secret of even the secrets of the five families consisting of that [reality] is the Pañḍākinī. For instance: the Lords of the Families (kuleśas) are characterized by the light that pervades their own respective families;
therefore, they are coarse (audārika).
Because the aspect of existence (bhāva) is predominant,
the Ḍākinīs are characterized by the emptiness of duality within that very light;
therefore, they are subtle.
Because they consist primarily of limbs that are non-existent;
among those [mantras] which are most secret of the secret, Mahāmāyā is the secret.
For it is thus: they are gross because they are characterized by the nature of each individual family (kula).
This, however, is the *dharmatā* common to the five families; it is the equality of all five of them.
Therefore, this is the secret even of those [five], and thus it is the supreme secret.
Because it expresses that, this *tantra* is also called the "Supreme Secret."
Let the supreme secret be told.
To the question "How is she called Mahāmāyā?", he says: "Mahāmāyā," and so forth.
For she is indeed most fierce (*mahāraudrā*).
Because she is supremely destructive.
Why? Because she effects the destruction of the elements (*bhūta*).
Since they are not truly produced (*abhūtatvāt*), "the elements" refers to all obscurations to the awakening of a Buddha.
She is the one who effects its withdrawal, the bringer of dissolution;
for that dissolution is supreme liberation.
Thus it is considered: she is called *māyā* because she measures (*mīnāti*).
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1477, kryādi-gaṇa]. There is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel] when the suffix *ṇ* follows. ||5||
By her all the three worlds, including everything mobile and immobile, were pervaded;
she is this very one who destroys the universe and creates it again and again.
She is the mother of the Guhyakas, renowned as Mahāmāyā;
she is the accomplisher of the three worlds and the bestower of all desires. (7)
He states another method, beginning with "yayā" and so forth.
"The three worlds" refers to the completely pure buddha-field, including all moving and non-moving beings, as previously described (p. 4), because [the deity] pervades it, having arisen from it.
For that is indeed the Dharma-body,
and this entire world of moving and non-moving things is its emanation.
Thus, it is considered that [the Buddha] "creates" through illusion (māyā).

Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṇa* [is applied] to the root *māṅ* 'to measure' (DhP 1088)," he states another alternative by means of the passage beginning with "sā punaḥ" ("as for that, moreover").
The word "punaḥ" means "furthermore."
The meaning is "another method.
"She herself" refers to Mahāmāyā in the form of Heruka.
"She withdraws the three worlds," it says.
Because he reduced Maheśvara and the others to ashes by the fall of his glance,
yet afterwards created them again, having purified them of their faults by reviving them with the sounds of great banners and bells. ||6||
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the Guhyakas," and so forth.
The deities in the external Vajra family are called Guhyakas because they are secret (guhya).
She is their mother.
The meaning is "mother.
For this reason, she is renowned and celebrated as Mahāmāyā.
The sense is that by adding the suffix *ṇapratyaya* to the roots *miñ* and *māṅ*, it is formed as previously explained (pp. 5–6).
Let this [nature] remain as it is;
however, what does it do for practitioners? To this he says: "The three worlds," and so forth.
It is called *vidhā* because its essential nature is unsurpassed knowledge (*niruttara-jñāna*).
This rite known as Mahāmāyā accomplishes the three worlds for practitioners; it bestows all desires and all attainments, such as the state of a vidyādhara,
in an excellent manner.
By means of which, through the method of the Lord of Accomplishers consisting of mere consciousness,
[one perceives] those who are gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and humans.
Vidyādharas, Guhyakas, Kinnaras, Mahodaras, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas indeed become accomplished for the sake of practitioners. 9.
All beings, whether born of water or land, are brought under control;
for all phenomena are luminous by nature, primordially pure, and indeed unclouded. (10)
This half-verse is the brief statement (*uddeśa*);
its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) begins with "by this" (*anena*) [1.8],
and so forth, up to "by this method of *yogamāyā*" [1.10].
16) This concludes [the section].
By whatever method she is the Mistress of Accomplishers (*sādhakeśvarī*), that is, the teacher of the practitioners (*sādhaka*), merely by being instructed— that is,
by the mere act of being made known— [she is so called].
The connection is that they are accomplished for practitioners. To the question "Who are they that are accomplished?", he says: "Devas," and so forth.
Devas are Śakra and others;
Dānavas are those with great supernatural power (*mahardhika*) among the pretas.

The Gandharvas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and others are so called because they exist together with Yakṣas and other beings. For the practitioners (*sādhaka*), they become subject to their will, as they bring about the success (*siddhi*) of those practitioners. (8–9)
"Subservient" (vaśyam) means being subject to command. "Beings" (bhūtāni) refers to sentient creatures.
"Water-born" refers to crocodiles and other such aquatic animals.
"Land-born" refers to tigers and the like.
Thus far, the means for accomplishing this external triple world have been indicated.
Now, in order to indicate the means for accomplishing even the supramundane triple world, he says: "The primordial nature," and so forth.

Here, the causal tantra (*hetutantra*) is stated briefly by means of half a verse; the resultant tantra (*phalatantra*) by the line of the verse beginning with "of the self-arisen ones possessing the five gnoses" (1.11); and the method tantra (*upāyatantra*) by the third, fifth, and sixth lines.
*Prakṛti* is one's own inherent nature; by that [nature], they are luminous (*prabhāsvara*), meaning they have the quality of shining, or in other words, they are exceedingly pure.
He asks, "What, then, are they? and replies: "Dharmas.
Dharmas are those which maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
the meaning is that they are all things.
Furthermore, all these entities are mind-only,

because it is the mind itself that appears in those various forms. For example, in a dream, houses, palaces, ponds, elephants, horses, humans, and so forth— though appearing as many— are indeed specific manifestations of the mind.
And it is said in the *Daśabhūmika*: "This triple world is mind-only" (p.
32). It is also said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: "An external object does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish."
"The mind, stirred by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), arises as the appearance of objects" (10.154–155).
"Stirred by latent impressions" means afflicted by latent impressions; that is to say, it is corrupted.
Let all phenomena be mere consciousness;
however, as for the question "from what [source] are they luminous and radiant by their very nature?", he says: "Ādi," and so forth.
"Ā" is the beginning of the beginning (*āderādiḥ*), meaning from the very outset.
They are pure because of the absence of all veils and impurities; they are untroubled because of the absence of the latencies of those impurities.
The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "yasmāt" (because).
Because they are pure from the very beginning, they are therefore luminous by nature; because of the three tasks, they are therefore luminous by nature.
[Objection: But while the impurities and their latent impressions (vāsanās) are being removed, how can they be pure and stainless?
Therefore, because the stains of intrinsic natures are adventitious therein— just as darkness, frost, smoke, clouds, and dust are in space—
they are thus naturally luminous.
If it were not so, there would be no awakening for anyone, because the stains that are the intrinsic nature of the mind cannot be exhausted as long as consciousness exists.
Therefore, the luminosity of the nature of consciousness is the cause of awakening; [it is] awakening.
Therein, the means are proclaimed for the self-arisen ones who possess the five knowledges;
[they are] the Yoginī and the Mother of Yoga, throughout the three realms without exception. (11)
The fruit: that awakening, moreover, is the ultimate purification of the mental continuum through the exhaustion of all obscurations along with their latent predispositions;
it is itself the *dharmakāya*.
Because it is the body, the dwelling, and the support for those phenomena comprised within the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies. ||10||

In that regard, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are self-arisen by virtue of their *dharmakāya*; because they manifest solely through their own nature due to the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) resulting from the removal of all obscurations, they possess the five gnoses.
Their five gnoses are as follows: the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*),...
the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment,
and the wisdom of accomplishing activities.

And the knowledge of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Among these, the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*) is like a mirror: stainless, infinite, and eternal; it is the support for the three middle knowledges and the locus where the reflections of all other knowledges arise.
Through the arising of which reflection the Tathāgatas become seers of all phenomena in all their aspects;

the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), which is the knowledge of the non-distinction between oneself and all sentient beings, and is always conjoined with great loving-kindness and great compassion;

the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which is unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge, the treasury of all meditative concentrations and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), and the exhibitor of all its own manifestations within the circles of the Dharma.
It is the showerer of the great rain of the Dharma.

That gnosis by which Tathāgatas, in all world-systems, perform the welfare of infinite sentient beings at every moment through infinite manifestations of body, speech, mind, and nirvāṇa— that is their gnosis of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

By means of that gnosis through which the Tathāgatas perceive the perfectly pure suchness of all phenomena— because they see only that [suchness] and because all stains of signs no longer appear at all—
Thus, these constitute their knowledge of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu.
The first three knowledges are the saṃbhogakāya;
the fourth is the nirmāṇakāya.
The fifth is a portion of the Dharmakāya;
they are self-arisen,
and all magical transformations, without exception or remainder, are accomplished by them.
He takes away [the merit] of all the Buddhas and enjoys the foremost maidens of the gods. ||12||
They are thus called "possessors of the five gnoses," meaning the Tathāgatas. The means for attaining those who have become the fruit are here praised— that is, they are primarily taught.

In that context, while that cause—namely, the intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*)—exists, this result occurs even without the means (*upāya*); for if [the result were produced] solely by the cause, since the cause is beginningless, it would follow that everyone would attain awakening from the very outset. Therefore, the means are praised. To the question "What are they?", he says: "The Yoginī," and so forth.
"Yoginī" refers to the five ḍākinīs; "Yogamātā" refers to Mahāmāyā;
and "the entire three realms without exception" refers to the whole of the triple world.
And how are these lords of the families (kuleśas) produced here within the families, and how do these families comprise the triple world?
Furthermore, how are these skillful means (upāyas) included within the secrets of the Tathāgatas in the three vajra-realms?

Because when the cause is complete, there is the potential for enlightenment characterized by fitness; through the cultivation of these very [means], along with the equipment such as birth and so forth, enlightenment is swiftly attained. Thus, this is the truth.

And once that [Buddhahood] has been attained, by means of these very [qualities] comprised within the enjoyment body and the emanation body, one brings others to the attainment of the three types of enlightenment according to their respective capacities. ||11||
"It is accomplished" means that it is brought to completion for practitioners by means of both the path and the fruit through the mere realization of which [this occurs].
"Without remainder, entirely" means that these very three groups, beginning with the *yoginīs*, are "entirely" because not even a single group is abandoned.
Because of not abandoning even a single deity, it is "without remainder" (aśeṣam); and because that [non-abandonment] is complete and exhaustive, it is "entirely without remainder" (tanniḥśeṣā).
Why is it accomplished?

Because all miraculous transformations are entirely dependent upon Mahāmāyā during both the stages of the path and its fruition; thus, yogis, lords of yoga, and creators perform [these feats] like a magical illusion.
Delusion, immobilization, as well as killing, expulsion, and so forth. ||13||
The rites of subjugation and attraction, as well as traveling through the sky, activities such as entering another's body, and [powers] such as invisibility. ||14||
That which was previously indicated as "the achiever of the three worlds" (1.7) has now been explained.
That which was indicated as "the bestower of all desires" (1.8)...
7) That too has been pointed out by the statement beginning with "it takes away" (*harate*) and so forth.
It takes away— that is, it draws toward itself— either for its own sake or for the sake of another.
"Buddhānām" means of the Buddhas. "Bhuṅkte" means he draws forth and enjoys. "Surāgrāḥ" means the foremost among gods, such as Śakra and others. ||12||
Yogas are concentrations (*samādhi*). Mastery over them is the power of sovereignty (*vaśitva*) for both entering into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and emerging from it.
Mahāmāyā is threefold.
Indrajāla is the creation and display of armies and the like, as well as their appearance and disappearance according to circumstances, whether they be real or unreal;
it is also delusion, which produces fainting.
Stambhana is the act of immobilizing. Māraṇa is the killing of those who cause extreme harm to the Three Jewels and so forth. Uccāṭana is the expulsion from one's place.
By the word "etcetera," [it is meant] the breaking of limbs, fever, possession by grahas, possession by rākṣasas, and so forth. ||13||
"Subdued" (*vaśya*) means having come under control;
however, in this context, the ritual action for the purpose of subduing is called "subduing.
Regarding the two types of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*): there is the attraction of the feet and the attraction of the physical body (*piṇḍa*).
The first is performed with the earth, the second with space;
these three rites are rites for subjugation and attraction.
"Entering another's body" (parapura) is expressed by the term *parapura*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [powers] such as the power of exiting the body (*vyutkrānti*) are included.
These very [powers] are the effects, namely the effects of entering another's body and so forth (*parapurādikāryāṇi*).
"By means of disappearances" means by means of invisibilities. ||14||
The crushing of those who bear enmity, as well as the ability to travel to the netherworld (pātāla), the sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, and likewise freedom from old age and death. ||15||
And there is freedom from disease for one who knows the yoga-illusion;
for yogis indeed transform even the imperishable into the form of mantra. 16.
Even for those who are mutually enamored,
causing estrangement is a means of liberation; entering a hole is going to Pātāla.
He who is the sovereign of the vidyādharas,
capable of both restraining and favoring them, is the Great Vidyādhara;
his state is "thatness" (tattva).
"Agelessness, immortality, and freedom from disease"—
these three are easily understood. And the word "and" (ca) implies "freedom from disease" as well.
All this, beginning with delusion (mohana), is performed by him through this method of *yogamāyā*; "is performed" is the ellipsis. *Māyā* refers to *mahāmāyā*.
The term *vidha* means "kind" (*vidhaiva vidhaḥ*);
the "union" (*yoga*) is the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of all the qualities of a Buddha; and this union is also the "kind of illusion" (*māyāvidha*).
The half-verse beginning with *vidhādhare* consists of seventeen syllables, while that beginning with *nirvyādhi* consists of fourteen syllables.
Regarding these, certain applications for all the activities such as seizing the qualities of all Buddhas are found in this very tantra. (2)
3. These points are to be explained. Some are to be understood according to other [sources]. It has been stated: "by consciousness alone" (1).
8) The meaning is "by means of the *anuṣṭhī*.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate its performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), he says "in the *akṣara*" and so forth.
The meaning is: by that which is both the *akṣara* and the form of the mantra, [he performs] those [rites].
The yogins, who are practitioners, perform transformations and sport by means of the attainments of karma and so forth. ||15-16||
They recite, contemplate, and cultivate through meditative concentration;
that which has been recited accomplishes the rites and shall bring about the attainment of the ritual goals. ||17||

Neither vows, nor unbearable asceticism, nor fasting, nor restraint lead to accomplishment; rather, they are always perfected through wisdom, skillful means, and the like, accompanied by joy and delight.
He explains how they practice the syllables (akṣara): "They recite" and "they contemplate. Here, "reciting" is muttering with speech;
"contemplating" is muttering with the mind.
He explains how those whose form is mantra perform [their practice], beginning with the words "visualizing" (bhāvayanti) and so forth.
"They cultivate" means they see by means of a continuous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
"by means of meditative concentration" (*samādhi*) means by means of the stability of the mind which has that as its object.
With the words beginning with "recited," he states the fruit of the practice—namely, "recited."
Having recited the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) according to the prescribed method,
she performs all rites, such as summoning and so forth.
By the second word, *vidhā*, the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) is expressed.
This, moreover, is the clear vision of oneself in the form of one’s own deity, which is the perfection of the cultivation of the [deity's] form.
It brings about for the practitioner the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*).
By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), one should also accomplish the ritual actions (*karmāṇi*).
The accomplishment of oneself in the form of one's own deity, both by oneself and by others, is the attainment of Mahāmudrā. ||17||
He states the ease of performance [in the passage beginning with] "not," and so forth.
Here, the word "not" implies "one should cause [others] to do," meaning one should not do it oneself.
The rule consists of bathing three times, changing clothes three times, and so on.
Subsisting on vegetables, barley-gruel, and other such food is austerity (*tapas*). Intolerance is suffering (*kaṣṭa*).
This is the instruction.
The explanation of this very [term] is "fasting" (*upavāsa*) and "restraint" (*saṃvara*). Therein, fasting is the abstaining from food;
restraint is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) even for a householder with intense passion.

The sensations that are beneficial are those born together with the five sensory consciousnesses, which are pleasures; those born together with the mental consciousness are joys. By means of these, the Hero, abiding in the center of the navel within the range of the pericarp and the anus, is the mind that is no-mind, the state of pure consciousness, whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge. (19)
The practitioners attain accomplishment.

The Great Ḍākinī consisting of meditative cultivation, or an external woman who has been cultivated by that [meditation], is the Wisdom (prajñā). The Means (upāya) for her is tranquility; it is the enjoyment [of her] by means of one's own self cultivated in the form of Śrī Heruka.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the five offerings and the five qualities of sensual pleasure are also included.
"With them always" means at every twilight. ||18||
How, then, is there joy and delight through wisdom and means? He says: "The navel," and so forth. It is the lotus of the navel; [the deity] resides in its center.
To the question "Who is he?", he says: "The Hero.
Because of his possession of unsurpassed heroism (*vīrya*), the Hero is Vajrasattva.
To the question "In what vessel does he reside there?", he says: "The pericarp," and so forth.

The term *gudagocara* refers to that which is within the scope of the *guda* (the anus) of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the navel-lotus; that is, it is located in the region of the pericarp and the anus.
*Guhana* means the anus, and *gupti* means concealment; the term *gocara* signifies a vessel for that purpose, hence it is called *gudagocara*.
The meaning is that it is the "enclosure" (*saṃpuṭa*) of the sun and the moon.
By this much, its location and vessel have been described.
He states its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) with the words beginning with "mind" (*citta*).
"Citta" means consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The words "san" and "kevala" are restrictive (*avadhāraṇa*) particles.
For example: "one who subsists on air alone" (*vāyubhakṣaḥ*).
One who subsists on air alone is called "air-eater" (*vāyubhakṣa*);
likewise here too, because there is no object of perception existing apart from consciousness, the meaning of the word "mind" (*citta*) is that the universe is mind-only.
Furthermore, even that mind is non-mind (*acitta*).
Why [is there no mind]? Because of the absence of an object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Why [is there no mind]? Because of the absence of an object of apprehension.
Why is that? Because in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is also an absence of a grasper.
Now, in the world, consciousness (vijñāna) is well known as the grasper; and here, "mind" (citta) is precisely this consciousness.
Therefore, it is both mind and non-mind, hence "mind-and-non-mind.

If it is non-mind because it is devoid of the characteristic of mind as a subject (grāhaka), then by virtue of being endowed with which characteristic of mind is it mind? To this he says: "having the nature of consciousness" (cidrūpa).
Consciousness is *cit*; manifestation is *prakāśa*;
appearing is *sphuṭatva*.
"In immediate presence" (aparokṣatā) is the meaning. That is its form; thus it is "of the nature of consciousness" (cidrūpa).
Because of its connection with the characteristic of being consciousness through its having the nature of consciousness, the meaning is that it is "the mind" (citta).
Now, one might object: "Is not all consciousness of this very nature?
What, then, is the excellence of the hero's own-being (vīrasvabhāva)? To this, he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.
*Sva* means one's own; *rūpa* means form; thus, *svarūpa*.
"Knowledge and the object of knowledge" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
That which has knowledge and the object of knowledge as its very nature is "that whose nature consists of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known.
That which is known is the "knowable" (*jñeya*).
In this context, even the intrinsic nature of the cognitions of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) is a knowable,
because they conceptually construct both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, even though these two do not exist.
For even though they are not real entities, the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender appear within them;
and that which does not exist, nor is a real entity, [does not appear].
That is not the innate nature of that consciousness;
rather, it is superimposed by error.
For this very reason, it is called the cause of error.
Because of the nature of the deluded mind:
for those to whom the non-essential nature is the object of knowledge, their cognition also becomes non-essential in nature.
Namely, it is appearance (bhānti). For instance: by virtue of appearance, even that which is non-existent or a non-entity appears; therefore, that [appearance] is also cognition.
It is renowned as the cause;
however, that error is the innate nature of the intellect,
whereas the impurities are adventitious.
Therefore, their cognition is also devoid of intrinsic nature.
Ultimate bodhicitta, however, consists of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*).
Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is delusion.
Therefore, because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are absent therein,
his cognition is his very own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and not even an illusion;
for all causes of conceptual proliferation have set there, and thus do not appear.
Its very own nature (*svarūpa*) alone is to be known,
not even that of non-existent things.

Thus, by this half-verse, the essential nature (*svabhāva*)— consisting of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*)— which is the characteristic of ultimate bodhicitta, has been directly stated.
However, its nature as great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is stated by implication,
because great bliss is co-emergent with non-conceptual gnosis (*nisprapañca-jñāna*).
Thus it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*:

Having become one whose intention is free from conceptual construction regarding this true Dharma, the Son of the Victor transcends the difficult terrain of conceptualization and gradually attains the state beyond conceptualization.
I shall explain that *vīra* within the profound teaching of the Buddha;
having arranged the vowels and consonants there, one should form a triple enclosure of lines. (20)
"Tranquil, immovable, supreme, under one's own control, equal to the unequaled, and consisting of non-conceptual bliss—therefore, the bodhisattva attains it. Thus [it is said].
In this pair of verses, "one whose intention is non-conceptual" means one whose intention is firm; "in this true Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna.
"Son of the Victor" refers to the bodhisattva.
"Difficult passage" refers to the fourfold conceptual construction itself;
having gradually transcended—that is, passed beyond—it.
"One attains the non-conceptual" means that one attains non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
From that very knowledge, one attains non-conceptual bliss;
it is "tranquil" because it is free from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*).
It is immovable, because it is non-retrogressive;
it is supreme, because it excels all mundane and supramundane happiness;
it is sovereign, because it can be manifested at will and for as long as desired.
It is equal—that is, identical—to other pleasures by way of its class as pleasure; it is unequal to these very four [other] distinctions. ||19||
I shall describe such a hero.
To the question "In which vehicle is he renowned?", he says: "In the Buddha's teaching" (buddhaśāsane).
That by means of which vehicle one becomes a Buddha is the Buddha's teaching.
The meaning is "in the Mahāyāna.
Now, one might object: "Has this not already been stated by the preceding verse? Why then do you say 'I shall explain'? To this, he says: "profound" (gambhīra).
"In the profound Mahāyāna" means in the Mantra-yāna.

For in the Mantra system, which is distinct from the Pāramitā-naya, the form of the seal (*mudrā*) and the determination of the *bodhicitta* are cultivated as more rapid means for achieving enlightenment.
And that has not yet been stated;
therefore he says, "I shall explain.
He explains that very point with the words beginning with "āli-kālī" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "therein," it means she is joined for the purpose of being constrained within the union of the sun and the moon. To the question "Where? he replies: "In the line. From that very boon, a ray of light has arisen through the subtle aperture in the center of the moon; it is an indivisible, uncut line of radiance as fine as a lotus fiber.

How is she directed? Having made that very [line] equal to the *āli* and *kālī*—the *āli* and *kālī* being the equal, blazing, upward-facing line, and beneath it the downward-flowing one—it flows as semen in the form of nectar in the form of a drop. (21)
That [lineage] is called "such" (tathoktā). How are those [teachings] in it?
Because they are strung together in that very [lineage] by means of a pearl necklace.
How are they equal?
Because two half-kālīs are expressed by the word "kālī," since they are parts of a single kālī.
These [vowels] also consist of sixteen syllables, due to the exclusion of ṅ and ñ;
therefore, there is equality between them.
And that line of rays encloses the *saṃpuṭa* with three coils.
Upon it, the three lines (*āli*) of the moon are strung together according to the recitation.
Therein, in the center, is the row of vowels (*svarālī*), and on either side of these are the two half-rows (*ardhākālī*).
And thus it will be said: "With divine lines of syllables" (1.26).
And it is stated in the *Śrīsaṃvarottara*:
One should arrange the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *da*, excluding *ṅa* and *ña*;
one should then draw the two *ali*s (vowels) beginning with *dha* and ending with *kṣa*.
"But the row of vowels, situated in the center, is to be placed upon the lunar disc. (20)
"Blazing," and so forth:
when another line of rays, blazing with the fire of the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*), emerges from the *virāj*, then it becomes that which causes downward flow.
For here, the meaning of "sruti" is expressed by the word "sruti," which means "flowing. Now, he asks: what flows within that flow? He says: "the nectar (amṛta)."
It is called "immortal" (amṛta) because of its liberated state, its indestructibility, and its great bliss.
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "having the form of a drop" (bindurūpiṇam).
The meaning is that the Hero is a white drop, having the nature of the mind of great bliss.
He explains how it flows: "in the form of semen.
The essence of pure gnosis is designated by the word "semen" because of its similarity to semen, owing to its white color and liquid nature.
It flows in that form.
It flows;
that is to say, it trickles away.
Thus, by means of the sequence beginning with *alikālī*, the extreme fragility of the *virāma* has been stated here.
By the words beginning with "blazing" (jvalitā), the ritual action (karma) is indicated;
by the word "nectar" (amṛta), another essential nature (svabhāva) is indicated;
and by the phrase "having the form of a drop" (bindurūpiṇam), its seal-form (mudrākāra) is described.
How, then, does this become his seal? It is said: that white moon which is the subtle bindu is the mind (citta).
Because it is luminous within.
Furthermore, that which is the mind’s abiding in that alone is "mind-only" (cittamātratā), due to the non-perception of any object distinct from the mind.
That state of being a non-apprehender which belongs to it due to the absence of an apprehended object is its lack of mind;
for this very reason, it has the nature of emptiness.
Furthermore, that which is its luminosity is its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*).

Moreover, for one whose mind is established in that alone, the subsiding of all signs of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is its nature as both knowledge and the object of knowledge (*jñānajñeyarūpatā*).
And this is the form of the subtle wisdom-mudrā of this Vajradhara. It is also stated in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"One should meditate on a moon-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-element."
Having visualized the form of the Buddha, one should commence the subtle yoga.
"One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose;
within that mustard seed, one should meditate upon the delightful state of gnosis, the secret fashioned by knowledge. Thus it is said.
In the *Śrīvajrāmṛta* as well, this common yoga of his, together with its ritual action, is established thus:
"One should remain motionless and begin the meditation on the nectar of knowledge;
one meditates upon the supreme reality, the nectar in the form of a drop."
In the center of the sky, the reality of emptiness is proclaimed, resembling the moon—
indestructible, immutable, subtle, the unstruck Vajrasattva.
"The God, situated in the center of the navel within the region of the pericarp,
flows in the form of semen, stationed between the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*. Therefore,
it is recited in such a manner.
In this regard, both yoga and action are exactly of that same nature;
for whatever sense-faculty may proceed along its path, it does so by virtue of its own inherent nature, since everything is composed of the Buddha through the yoga of supreme absorption. (22)
Now, one might object: "In this tantra, it is taught that four wheels (*cakras*) are to be meditated upon in four locations, not Caṇḍālī?

Is it not by her, blazing forth, that the fourfold wheel is set ablaze, and having emerged and expanded, she heats the four wheels of all the Buddhas, then returns and enters the Great Bliss Wheel (*mahāsukhacakra*), causing the nectar to flow from the syllable *Haṃ*?
To this, some reply that all of this has been seen elsewhere and is merely being established here [by us].
That is incorrect,
because there is no expressive authority [for it] and because all systems have diverse intentions.
And because this tantra is characterized by a very concise essential principle. ||21||
With the words beginning "whatever," he describes another ritual act:
the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, should go— that is, attain— the state of being paths, which is to say, the state of being objects.
Whatever may exist, whatever may be seen,
heard, or smelled—
It should be tasted and touched; one should ascertain that all this consists of the Buddhas, each and every thing being of the nature of no Buddha whatsoever.
How does it consist of all the Buddhas?
"By way of intrinsic nature" means by its own nature, that is to say, by its primordial essence (*prakṛti*).
For thus the *dharmadhātu*, which is without beginning or end, is the primordial essence of all phenomena.
And that very dharmadhātu is the supreme form of all Buddhas.

Therefore, by virtue of that intrinsic nature, that reality consists of all Buddhas—not only by its own nature, but also through its connection with the supreme benefit [of others]. Even without that [connection], one is liberated through the realization of the ultimate goal.

Supramundane gnosis is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and is characterized by detachment; the meaning is that it is the supreme benefit produced by the means established through that [gnosis], namely, the state of being free from conceptual proliferation. "Union" (*yoga*) with that is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
The meaning is that by means of this resolve—that the visible objects and so forth appearing in perception and the like are indeed devoid of essence and motionless—[one attains stability]. ||22||
The accomplishment of the great samaya is indeed the practice of the great pill;
one should perform the yoga-vow by means of the applications of Mahāmāyā. ||23||

Through the fivefold offerings of worship and likewise through the five strands of sensual pleasure, it should be known by the lords of the Siddhas and others that the accomplishment is eternal and imperishable. (24)
With the words "Mahāsamaya" and so forth, he describes another ritual action.
*Samaya* refers to the deity;
the *mahāsamaya* is the lord of the mandala, who is together with the mandala (*samaṇḍala*).
Its accomplishment (*siddhi*) is its manifestation.
The particle *ti* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
That accomplishment is the practice of the Great Pill (*mahāgulikā-sādhana*); the pill (*gulikā*) is the Drop of Knowledge (*jñānavindu*).
The retinue consists of four drops;
the central drop is the great pill (mahāgulikā);
by that, there is accomplishment (sādhana), which is the production [of the deity].
The accomplishment of the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*).
To the question, "Once the maṇḍala has been accomplished, what should one do?", he says "Mahāmāyā," and so forth.
The Lord of the Maṇḍala, Śrī Heruka, is Mahāmāyā.
The consort of that [deity] is also the Buddha-Ḍākinī Mahāmāyā,
because the two possess a single nature.
Through their ritual applications— namely, the actions of embracing, kissing, and so forth— one should practice the yoga-vow (*yoga-saṃvara*).
Yoga and Saṃvara constitute the Yoga-Saṃvara.
Therein, "yoga" refers to the subtle white moon situated within the union of the sun and moon at the pericarp of the navel-lotus.
"Saṃvara" is the supreme bliss, the great bliss (*mahāsukha*); its function consists of penetration and analytical investigation.
By the verse beginning with "jvalitā" and so forth, that which was previously stated [in 1.21] is [reaffirmed]. ||23||
Is it only this alone?
No, he says—“the five,” and so forth.
The meaning is that it is accompanied by these ten.

Therefore, from that very semen of gnosis (*jñānaretas*), there is the sequential emanation of ten clouds—flowers and so forth—that individually pervade the sky and reside within the lotus-womb of the *ḍākinīs*.
They are called "offerings" (*apahāra*) because they are presented; these are the flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and food offerings (*naivedya*).
Those not yet attained which are desired or longed for are called *kāmāḥ*; those already attained which are cherished or enjoyed again are called *guṇāḥ*.
These objects of desire are the "qualities of desire" (*kāmaguṇāḥ*), and they are excellent.
O Goddess, I shall tell you that knowledge by which, once perfected, one may swiftly reach the abode of the thirty gods;
I swear this truth to you. (25)
Therefore, I shall [teach] to you that great illusion, the lore which accomplishes the three worlds—the divine [lore] of the great yogins, indeed, through its series of imperishable syllables. (26)
These are form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Among these, the secret worship and the jewel worship constitute the internal restraint (*saṃvara*);
the remaining ones are external worship.
Regarding this worship of the deity, he states the fruit [of the practice] with the words beginning "jñātavyam" (it is to be known).
It is to be known—that is, it is to be ascertained.
Because it is an indeclinable [particle], it is absolute...
Because it is inexhaustible, the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrāsiddhi) is eternal;
"I shall attain that" is the remainder of the sentence. ||24||
Having thus briefly explained meditation along with its benefits, he now describes the recitation (*jāpa*) accompanied by common benefits, beginning with the words "by which" (*yena*).
"By knowledge" (*jñānena*) means by the *vidyā*.
"By the perfected" (*siddhena*) means by that which has been practiced.
The "thirty-three" are the gods;
their abode is their dwelling place.
"O Goddess" is an address to the Buddha-Ḍākinī.
To the question "Is this true or not?", he says "It is true," and so forth.
An emphasis is understood here;
the meaning is: "I speak only the truth, never a falsehood. (25)
To the question, "What then is that knowledge? Which deity is it, what is its power, and what is its nature? he says: "That I... and so forth.
In the phrase "you" (*tvām*) and so on, the accusative case is used because of its connection with the verb "I shall speak" (*vakṣyāmi*).
To the question "Which deity? the answer is: "The great illusion, the Vidyā. To the question "Of what power? the answer is: "The accomplisher of the three worlds.
To the question "Of what nature? the answer is: "Divine to the great yogins."
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
"Divya" means that in which one plays; it refers to the secret [place], namely the union of the sun and the moon (*ravisomasaṃpuṭa*).
For that is their state of equality;
therefore, that alone is the locus of delight for yogins.
"By means of rows of syllables" refers to the three rows consisting of vowels and consonants.
The word "adorned" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The hero situated in its center is Śrī Heruka;
he, moreover, is the "enclosed" one, meaning Buddhaḍākinī. ||26||
By the mere thought of this, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is accomplished;
and one is served with the enjoyment of all desires according to one's wish. ||27||
For the great yogi, sporting [in this way], always attains success in the auspicious;
and through yoga, they manifest themselves in various forms and appearances. (28)
It bestows great accomplishment and brings about the glory of the Tathāgatas;
it always effects the welfare of sentient beings through various elixirs. (29)
Having brought forth semen and wine, as well as the great *piṇḍa* and the great meat, it is enjoyed together with the Yoginīs after they have brought them forth. (30)
"By which" means by that which is presided over by the union of the sun and moon, adorned with the three rows of vowels and consonants.
"Merely by thinking" means merely by reciting;
how the recitation is to be performed will be explained in the second instruction (2.12).
"Moving and non-moving" refers to the external triple world;
it is accomplished, meaning it becomes subject to his will,
as the yogin practices it.
By means of which Vajrayoginīs,
"according to their desire" (yathecchayā)— meaning whatever they wish— they "show," that is, they grant him a vision.
The mantra-deities are the self of yoga. ||27–28||
"Dadati" means "he gives.
He gives the eightfold great siddhi, such as the sword, collyrium, and so forth.
"Tāthāgatīm" means...
Because they have realized suchness, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called Tathāgatas; this is their *tāthāgatī*,
meaning glory or perfection.
"He who says 'do [this]' is that very yogin. ||29||
"Madyam" means the drawing in of intoxicants;
"āhṛtya" means having drawn in;
"āyuḥ" means life.
Vīrya is enthusiasm;
tejas is power;
and the divine eye is visual consciousness.
Day by day, he gains great longevity, great heroism, great splendor, and likewise strength, divine vision, and supernatural power, as well as the essence of Soma. (31)
He shall attain a vast lifespan lasting until the end of a great kalpa,
and he displays miracles with a form that is never-tiring to behold.
By mere mental recitation, she effects a transformation of one's own nature;
the Mistress of Vidyās, the bestower of great supernatural powers, she is the unfailing one whose success is attained through recitation alone. 33.
"And supernatural power" (ṛddhi) refers to the supernormal knowledge of psychic powers (ṛddhyabhijñā). "Soma-drink" is the drinking of nectar (amṛta). "Day by day" means every single day.
"He attains" is the remainder of the verse. ||30-31||
"Long life" was mentioned [in 1.31].
This is its detailed explanation: "He," and so forth.
That yogi would go to—that is, attain—vast, extensive life.
A *mahākalpa* is that which has this as its conclusion or limit, as it has been stated.
"He demonstrates" refers to the yogin.

It is called a *pratihārya* because by means of it sentient beings are led (*hriyante*) or summoned (*āvajryante*) back again and again (*prati prati*); the suffix *-aṇ* is used in the sense of the base word itself, thus it is a *prātihārya*.
And that is threefold: the miracle of supernatural power (ṛddhiprātihārya), the miracle of mind-reading (ādeśanāprātihārya), and the miracle of instruction (anuśāsanīprātihārya).
In order, there are three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*): psychic power (*ṛddhi*),
knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and [knowledge of] the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
And [he possesses] the knowledge of the future.
"He displays a body whose form is incomparable and which brings no satiety through the sight of it"—this is the connection with what precedes. ||32||

One's own nature (*svarūpa*) is the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*); its transformation (*parivartana*) is the assumption of another form (*pararūpaparigraha*). "Conceived by the mind" (*manasā cintitam*) means merely a mental discourse (*manojalpamātra*), such as "May I become like this."
O Upavidhi, there is nothing whatsoever equal to you in the three worlds by way of praise;
O beautiful one, this very tradition of the Tantras has been declared to you. (34)
Thus ends the first [chapter], the exposition of the signs for attaining the great vidyā of Yogeśvarī.
Concluding, he says: "The Mistress of Knowledge," and so forth.
The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the present tense (*vartamāne*), meaning that she is accomplished by the mere recitation [of her mantra].
Thus, the sense is that she grants success through simple repetition alone.
She is Amoghinī because her power is unfailing;
for when she is accomplished, she necessarily bestows the results as described. ||33||
"O two sciences!
There is no other science equal to you, like unto you, for me."
"In the three worlds" means in the three families of the Tathāgata, Vajra, and Padma. "Āgama" means the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
"O beautiful one" is the address. ||34||
She is Yogeśvarī by virtue of her aspect as means (upāya), and Mahāvidyā by virtue of her aspect as wisdom (prajñā). And who is she? She is Mahāmāyā.
Its accomplishment is its performance; its cause is its sign;
and its power is manifold.
Its explanation is the exposition.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Guṇavatī*, the commentary on the *Śrīmahāmāyātantra*.
The second exposition:
Now, therefore, I shall declare the divine [teaching] which bestows the fruit of yogic accomplishments for the Mahāyogeśvarīs. 1.
By whom, through mere thought, the desired boon is granted;
through the union of the first letters, he always performs the exhalation. (2)
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha ata" and so forth:
this is a single-line verse (*ekapadī gāthā*) consisting of twelve syllables.
The word *atha* serves to introduce the entirety of the recitation (*japa*).
"Therefore" refers to the meditation on the form of the deity;
"divine" refers to the Great Yoginīs. "Together with the heroes" means [the vessel] containing the heroes; the ellipsis is that one should contemplate [this] upon the pericarp of the navel-lotus.
Regarding what should be recited therein, he says "guhyā" and so forth.
It is called *guhyā* because it is not to be disclosed;
or alternatively, it is *guhyā* because by means of it the reality (*tattva*) of the deity is concealed.
The secret and that syllable;
yoga is the meditative absorption on the deity, and its accomplishment is its perfection.
The fruit is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which results from the very perfection of that [practice].
Because it bestows those two excellently, it is called "the bestower of the fruit of the accomplishment of yoga. (1)

"By mere recitation" (*japtimātreṇa*) means that even without the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), the desired boon—such as the state of a *vidyādhara* and so forth—is attained through recitation alone.
The intended meaning is that one should see the secret syllable within the cavity of the *sampuṭa*, and having raised the *virama* above it, one should perform the recitation.
To the question "How should one recite?", he says: "Beginning with... and so forth.
Here, the first syllable is the *praṇava*,
because it is generally seen at the beginning of mantras;
its application consists in its gradual recitation.
The connection is that the yogi performs this;
what does he perform? Exhalation, which is the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa). ||2||
Indeed, joined with the eighth vowel and the tilaka of the letter *ū*,
the yogi emits the breath that is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
"By the end of the eighth" means by the letter *ha*, which is the final member of the eighth group;
the connection is that "one should exhale."
How does one perform it?
By means of the letter *u*, such that it is joined beneath the letter *ha*,
and the letter *ha* is provided with a bindu (*m*) on its head.
The collective meaning is "by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
To the question of what kind of inhalation and exhalation one performs, he says: "devoid of existence and non-existence," with the words "in due order" being understood as the ellipsis.
For the meaning of the *praṇava* is indeed pure gnosis (*jñānamātratā*),
according to the statement in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*: "The syllable *oṃ* is the twofold gnosis" (11.2).

The meaning of the syllable *hūṃ* is the equality of body, speech, and mind by virtue of being without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), because it is stated in that very same [text]: “The syllable *hūṃ* brings about the body, speech, and mind as the indivisibility of the three vajras” (11.3).
Therefore, because of the vision of the universe— indicated by the syllable *oṃ*— as being nothing but mind (*cittamātratā*), it is "devoid of entities" (*bhāvavarjita*).
That very universe, which is mind-only, is non-existence (*abhāva*),
for there is no existence of entities apart from the mind.
The attainment of equanimity regarding that very universe of mind-only, which is the state of being free from appearances, is indicated by the syllable *hūṃ*.
From the vision of that, one is devoid of non-existence;
likewise, one is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
Then, what is the vision of "mind-only" (cittamātratā) and the attainment of equanimity?
Here is the instruction: while pronouncing the *praṇava* (OM), one should perceive a line of rays of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*) emerging along with the exhalation from the Hero (*vīra*).

Having pervaded all things by means of that [line], the transformation of the universe into the nature of the Buddha while pronouncing the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), and the visualization of that universe in the form of one's own deity, is the vision of mind-only.
Then, by means of the exhalation of the syllable *hūṃ*, there is the dissolution of the universe into the Hero (*vīra*) and the vision of the attainment of equanimity.
One should perform both of these again and again, very gradually, until weariness arises; this is what constitutes *jāpa* in this tantra. (3)
For him, there are no observances such as vows, nor constraints like the wearing of [ascetic] marks;
rituals such as fire-offerings and sacrifices—whether higher or lower—are all set aside. (4)
Yoga is said to be threefold, consisting of mantra, form, and dharma;
through this threefold knowledge, one is not stained by the defects of existence. ||5||
Thus, one who is constantly devoted to yoga and intent upon perpetual practice will, like Vajrasattva himself, attain accomplishment in a single month. (6)
Regarding this, he states the ease of practice with the words beginning "not for him" (*na tasya*):
"of him" refers to the one who is reciting; "vow" (*vrata*) refers to the observances such as silence, bathing, and dietary restrictions.

"Restraint" (yantraṇā) and "retention" (dhāraṇā) of the vital breath cease; that is, they do not continue according to other systems (tantrāntara). Furthermore, the sense of "one after another" is understood. The meaning is that all other external activities besides these also cease. ||4||
Now, is not recitation (japa) merely verbal utterance?

In this context, must the reciter perform only verbal utterance, or should there also be meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) regarding the form [of the deity] and its knowledge? To this, he says: "In the mantra," and so forth.
Yoga is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has reality as its object.
That yoga is threefold and of three types. Why? Because it consists of mantra, form, and the Dharma-nature.
Speech that illuminates reality is mantra;
the form of the deity together with its location is mūrti;
and knowledge of the meaning of the mantra is dharma.
"But by means of the threefold knowledge" refers to the three yogas just mentioned,
and not by mere verbal discourse alone.
"He is not smeared by the defects of existence" means that he is liberated from the faults of saṃsāra, such as sin and the like. ||5||
"Thus" refers to the three times of day;
"constantly" means every day;
"continually" means at each junction of the day (sandhyā).
"May it be accomplished! Thus it is fulfilled.
Vajrasattva [performs] the meditation on the first syllable conjoined with the color of Indra.
He draws him in an instant by means of that [mantra] encased within the Vidyā. ||7||
For by means of meditation joined with the second syllable, one may bring even the entire threefold world under one's control. ||8||
Śrī Heruka; equal to him means similar to him.
By the word "also" (api), it is implied that he is equal to Vajraḍākinī as well.
"Sa" refers to the yogin.
Therefore, in this context, one should meditate upon the form of Heruka and the knowledge-ḍākinīs through the pride of that identity.
As for the mantra, the syllables *praṇava* (oṃ) and *huṃ* are to be uttered slowly.
And in the midst of that, the root mantra is to be recited slowly.

One should understand the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra as follows: having raised the *virabindu* atop the syllables of the ritual procedure situated within the cavity of the union of the sun and moon, one should effect the transformation of all phenomena into the nature of the Buddha by means of the ray of light arising from it, and then dissolve them back into the *virabindu*.

Thus, when the recitation has been performed for six months through the application of mantras, forms, and dharmas, whether similar success has been attained or not, the ritual syllables, when correctly employed, necessarily accomplish their respective tasks. ||6||
In order to indicate the syllables of the injunction and their application, he says "indravarṇa," and so forth.
The *indragopa* is expressed by the word "indra.
The first syllable is the *praṇava*.
The practitioner should apply the meditation upon that [deity] for the purpose of summoning; thus,
being a practitioner of piercing yoga,
that yogi quickly brings the object of accomplishment under his control.
The explanation of "swiftly" (*kṣipram*) is "in an instant" (*kṣaṇāt*).

This is what is meant: having performed the yoga of Buddha-Ḍākinī and the others, which is reddish like saffron, one should contemplate the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) as reddish like saffron within the vessel of the *vīra*. Having placed the *vīra* within its lunar disc (*bindu*), and having turned the *vīra* red with the rays of the *praṇava*, one should draw forth two lines of reddish rays from the *vīra*. One should contemplate a noose at the tip of one [line] and a hook at the tip of the second.
One should visualize the target bound by a noose around the neck and pierced in the heart with a hook, being swiftly dragged forth;
thus, within a moment, he becomes drawn near. ||7||
"Second," and so forth.
In the *āli* reading, the second syllable is the letter *ā*;
therein reside Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and likewise Kāmeśvara.
Impelled by the syllable of ignorance, they are dragged away together with their wives. ||9||
Combined with forms and syllables, abiding in body, speech, and mind;
through the meditation on the threefold union, the supreme extraction of the *piṇḍa* is achieved. (10)

The hero, being thus applied, has his head raised; by that, the yogins of their own deity contemplate [the object] as consisting of atoms and color it. "Contemplation" (*vibhāvana*) refers to the contemplation to be accomplished through ritual procedure.
"And even all" refers to the phrase "the entire set of factors of the probandum," and so forth. The sense of "even" is understood;
it means that he brings even the entirety of the three worlds under his control.
What, then, is meant by "a hundred beings" or "a thousand beings"?

This means: having made the six [syllables] red like hibiscus through their conjunction, one should place the letter *Ā*—red like hibiscus—within the hollow of the hands (*sampuṭa*), and upon its head, the syllable *Vī*. Having colored the atoms of the person to be subdued with that very light, one should contemplate them as brought under control and fallen at one's feet.
All of them come under one's control. ||8||
"Beginning with Brahmā," etc.:
Kāmeśvara is Māra.
These [beings], beginning with Brahmā, are drawn forth.
Because it is inexhaustible (*akṣaya*), it is the syllable (*akṣara*); it is the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*). Its secret syllable is the imperishable syllable (*akṣarākṣara*).
In some places, the reading is *akṣarajñāna*;
in that case, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*).
The meaning is that the syllable *huṃ* abides in both;
and it is red as a hibiscus flower during the act of attraction,
being impelled— that is, set in motion— by that.
And how are they summoned? Like the practice of the first extraction.
Others say that the summoning here is by means of the exhalation of the syllable *huṃ*.
In this tantra, some say that all applications for summoning are performed with the trunks of rays of light arising from the *vīra*. 9.

He describes the supreme attraction of the *piṇḍa* with the words beginning with "ākāra": those joined with both the *ākāra* and the syllable (*akṣara*), or properly joined with the *ākāra*, that is, with the syllable *huṃ*, are the practitioners (*sādhakas*).
Having meditated upon oneself as four-faced, red and white, joined with the syllable *khe* and holding a skull in hand, there is the supreme attraction of semen (*śukra*). 11.
Having meditated upon oneself as the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva), joined with the syllable *ci* and yellow in color and radiant, this is the supreme method for summoning from the center. 12.
This is the meaning. "Threefold conjunction" (*trisaṃyoga*) refers to the conjunction with the three [factors].
"Situated in body, speech, and mind" means that it is established in the body, the throat, and the heart.

What is being said? Having made the yoga of any one of the six [syllables] swift and reddish, and having placed the *vīra* upon the head of the letter *Ā* or within the drop (*bindu*) of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one visualizes the wind-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *YAṂ*.

One should visualize the object of attainment (sādhya) with his neck bound by two lines of reddish rays from the Hero [deity] and pierced from below by a noose and a goad respectively, being swiftly drawn through the intermediate space;
in an instant, he becomes attracted. ||10||

"Khekāra," and so forth. This is what is meant: having visualized oneself as white, four-faced, holding a skull and a noose in hand, with a red mind, by means of the tube of rays arising from the *vīja* "KHE" situated at the head, which has entered the secret place of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), one should contemplate that his semen being drawn out is being placed within the skull.
"In an instant, she will be drawn forth," he said. ||11||
Regarding the passage beginning with "cikāre" and so forth:

having meditated upon the yellow-colored Hayagrīva, whose very self is yellow light, by means of the short syllable *ci*, one should contemplate drawing in the liquor contained in the vessel by means of the trunk of the Heroic Radiance (*vīraśmi*) situated at the head of the syllable *ci*. One should then imagine the vessel being filled;
thus, it becomes full in an instant. ||12||
Joined with the syllable *ra*, he is red in color and possesses great splendor;
he has four arms, four faces, the face of a jackal, and is well-established. ||13||
Having visualized oneself as wrathful, the supreme attraction of the blood [is performed], joined with the six-syllable mantra and applied to the six locations. (14)
The Vajra-Ḍākinīs, the Yoga, and the host of Ḍākinīs are accomplished;
likewise, the two eyes, the ears, the nose, and the heart. (15)
"With the letter *ra*, etc. means:

having visualized oneself as red-colored, four-armed, four-faced, with the face of a *jambu* tree, and of great splendor, and being wrathful; one should contemplate, as before, that blood is being drawn from the body of the target by means of a ray of light resembling a leech. ||13–13½||
In the yogas of one's own deity, this is the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of these very syllables of the injunction (*vidhyakṣara*).
Therefore, following the context, he also states that [placement] with the words beginning "six" (*ṣaḍ*):
the six syllables of the injunction mentioned immediately above are the six phonemes.
The connection is that one should contemplate [the body] as joined with those;
"the body of one's own deity" is the ellipsis.
To the question "joined with what?", he says: "in six locations."
The meaning is "in six locations.
This being so, the Vajrayoginīs are accomplished, and not otherwise.
Vajra is Heruka.
The yoginīs are the five ḍākinīs;
yoga is Śrī Heruka,
and his is the host of ḍākinīs.
Regarding the vow (*saṃvara*), it is stated that when there is supreme bliss together with those very *yoginīs*, it occurs in the six places of bliss.
He states those very places beginning with "the eye" (*cakṣuḥ*) and so forth.
For the mind is indeed the heart.
By virtue of the word "and," the tongue and the body [are also included]. 14–15.
Indeed, yogis bind the Siṃhavikrīḍitā mudrā;
having well-restrained their breath through prāṇāyāma and meditated, it blazes forth at that very moment.
Throughout the seven worlds, including the Akaniṣṭha heaven and all that is moving and unmoving, everyone meditates upon it, yet they do not truly understand it. ||17||
He states another yoga, beginning with "siṃha" and so forth:
"Siṃha" means a hero; that [mudrā] in which there is his playful sport (vikrīḍita) is thus described.
"Mudrā" means the union of the sun and moon;
"binding" means they contemplate it as bound by the three lines of syllables, as before. (1.26)
"Yogins" refers to those established in the yoga of Śrī Heruka surrounded by the four goddesses.
"Prāṇāyāma" refers to inhalation and exhalation.
"Suyantrita" means having properly restrained them.
The meaning is "having gradually made it subtle.
Regarding the word "having meditated":
having fixed the mind right there upon that which is visible through the opening of the moon's aperture, it blazes forth at that very moment. ||16||
For one whose mind has been stabilized in *vīra*, knowledge flashes forth instantly and produces illumination.
To the question of how far it flashes, he says: "through the seven worlds."
The netherworld (pātāla), the earth (bhū), heaven (svarga), the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth— these are the seven worlds;
their collection is "the seven worlds" (saptaloka),
which, like the term "the three worlds" (tribhuvana), is used in the neuter gender.
The first three dhyānas each consist of three stages,
while the fourth consists of eight stages;
its eighth stage is Akaniṣṭha.
Therefore, he says: "up to the world of Akaniṣṭha.
Therein, the mobile beings are the sentient beings (sattvas), while the immobile are the celestial palaces (vimānas), worlds (bhuvanas), and so forth.
Therefore he says: "moving and unmoving. Now, in order to show that this hero is visible to all sentient beings, he says: "visualizing," and so forth.
"All" refers to all sentient beings.
They cultivate and practice [this] so that,
if all perceive it as such within their own minds, the worldly play of existence perishes.
Therefore, this knowledge is secret, unmanifest, and beyond syllables.
For the perfectly awakened ones, having entered into yogic sleep, perceive [the world] as meditating on uniform forms, their minds absorbed in that single mass. (19)
Because it is seen to be so;
and because they do not perceive it, due to their failure to see reality, for that [reality] appears to the ignorant only through forms that are unreal. ||17||
The "play of the world" (*jagatkriḍā*)—the play of the universe consisting of the conceptualization of duality through various forms—would have perished previously;
yet it has not even now perished.
Because it is thus, therefore:
"This knowledge" refers to the reality of knowledge called Virā, which is non-dual;
"hidden" means concealed from the ignorant.
By whom? (Or: by what?)
By means of delusions that perceive unreal forms;
of what nature is it? It is unmanifest because it is beyond the range of speech, and it is syllable-less because it is not an object of mental discourse. ||18||
He states who, then, perceive this in the ultimate sense: "Those who understand," and so forth.
The word *hi* is used for emphasis and its position is displaced;
thus, it means "for those who are fully awakened" (*saṃbuddhā hi*).
The meaning is that they are indeed Tathāgatas.
If even the vision of the Tathāgatas were not established by their very nature, then it would be impossible for others to attain it.
Now, if it were dependent upon yoga, then others too might see him by means of that very same yoga; therefore, he says "by yoga," and so forth.
Because it is characterized by absolute lack of distraction, it is like sleep due to its similarity with sleep, and is thus called "sleep."
And having come together, being united with that yogic sleep; the description of that very state is "meditating," and so forth. "Forms" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).

For they meditate upon those [senses] which consist of the single flavor of mere luminosity free from appearances, arising from the nine gates and having the Buddha as their essence; indeed, the wise one should consume them with non-conceptual and intrinsic-less awareness. (20)
At the junction of the thumb and the ring finger, the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) resides;
it becomes of the nature of nectar, and eternal perfection is attained.
Thus ends the second instruction, titled "The Determination of Yoga" from the Great Tantra of the Lord of Yogins. || 2 ||
"Piṇḍa" means that very [reality] which, through extreme condensation—that is, through being made exceedingly subtle—is a mere *bindu*, as subtle as a mustard seed;
by this, the form of the *mudrā* of the *virāma* is established.
"Those whose minds are fixed on that" means:
With their minds fixed on that very same lump, this indicates the meaning of yogic sleep. ||19||
He states the rule (*samaya*) which is the cause for the accomplishment of such yogas, beginning with "they cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*).
"They cultivate" means they should have conviction (*adhimucyet*).
What should one have conviction in?
Regarding those objects that arise from the nine gates,
how should one resolve upon them?
The meaning is that they are of the nature of the Buddhas— the eternal, unshakeable Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Lokeśa, and Amoghasiddhi.
One should consume those very [concepts] for the purpose of consuming conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"By means of non-conceptualization" means without hesitation.
"By means of being without intrinsic nature" means by means of the absence of appearance regarding the grasped and the grasper.
"By the wise one" means by that which culminates in pure luminosity;
"by the mind" is the ellipsis. || 20 ||
"Thumb," and so forth.
"The wish-fulfilling gem at the gate" means that the cintāmaṇi is situated at the tips of the thumb and ring finger.
The sense is that one should then consume them by means of that very [power].
When? He says: "When it has become nectar," and so forth;
when all of that has become of the nature of nectar.
The meaning is "by the method that will be explained.
To the question "What would result from that?", he says: "Siddhi," and so forth. || 21 ||
It has been explained that *yogeśvarī* is the Great Vidyā (p. 24).
Her "union" (*ayoga*) is the union of the *bindu* within the enclosure of the Sun and Moon;
this is described by the passage beginning with "the lion’s play" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) and so forth. (2)
16) Its determination; its exposition is the explanation thereof.
Thus ends the second exposition in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyātantra*.
The third instruction:
Now I shall further proclaim other supreme means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), which are groups of substances to be consumed that bestow the fruit of omniscience. (1)
By the mere consumption of which the secret Mothers (Gūḍhamātaraḥ) are accomplished:
[the flesh] of an elephant, a man, a horse, as well as that of a cow and a dog. (2)
Combined with a great pala of the nectar of the five knowledges, these were cultivated for eight, ten, and up to fourteen days. || 3 ||
Having been kept for seven days by a jackal and then extracted, one should fashion five pills from those seeds, which are indeed called *siddhārtha*.
This has been properly concealed in other tantras; understanding it correctly yields great fruit.

"Others" means those different from the nine just mentioned. "Substance-groups" (*dravyagaṇa*) refers to those which are both substances and groups, because each one constitutes a portion of a group; [those].
"Omniscience" (*sarvajña*) refers to the state of being omniscient.
That very fruit [is obtained] from those who bestow it. || 1 ||
"By which" means by which collection of substances;
"the Vajra-Ḍākinīs are more secret. (2)
Endowed with greatness, adorned with great qualities, and possessing great fruit;
the word "tathā" (likewise) is used for conjunction.
"On the fourteenth day," and so forth.
On the eighth day, having smeared and dried them with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [one should do so] for seven days. || 3-4 ||
Likewise, on the eighth and fourteenth days,
having joined [the practice] in the midst of the Jambūka [cemetery],
one should then perform it in the midst of a Śivāṅga [cemetery] during the night of the Bhūtas.
Those white mustard seeds and fruits should be placed there. || 5 ||
The five substances as well as their measures are exactly as I have stated here in this tantra;
not everything has been stated in other tantras.
These great fruits have been concealed by means of intelligence.
"Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight"—
