when this has been done, "then, having joined them together" means having unified them.
"On the night of the spirits (bhūtarātrau), they are to be placed in the midst of the dog's body" means those items are to be established there.
Likewise, substances that have been thus cultivated and established are "siddhārtha fruits," being the size of mustard seeds. || 5 ||
He asks, "What, then, are those substances? and answers, "Five.
This means five palas. Likewise, it says, "of such measure."
And because it is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*), there is such a formulation; and regarding the phrase "and in the tantras" and so forth,
"not everything stated" means that not all has been spoken.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "It was concealed.
To the question "Having done what was it concealed?", he says: "Having understood them to be of great fruit.
The meaning is: having known those [teachings] to be of great fruit.
Whence the great fruits?

From the attainment of the state of identity with the Hero (vīrasārūpya) by means of the five aggregates, which have been cultivated through the five gnoses, which abide as the limbs of Śiva, and which reside within the vessel of the joined palms (sapuṭapātra). || 6 ||
Now, here is the means of accomplishment by which one should visualize the lotus of the mind, joined with the four goddesses, possessing a radiance equal to the color red. (7)
In the east, it has the luster of a blue lotus and is adorned with the image of a Buddha;
in the south, it is yellow in color, and in the west, it has a white radiance.
"Then," and so forth. "Then" means immediately following.
Herein, in this tantra, there is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*);
by which ritual action the Blessed One, together with his mandala, is accomplished—that is, propitiated.
"That becomes" means that it is produced from that.
Regarding "one should visualize the lotus":

having meditated on the world as equal to space through the cultivation of the non-manifest bodhicitta, and having contemplated the earth as consisting of vajras, one [visualizes] an eight-petaled and a four-petaled lotus within the interior of a peaked palace situated in the midst of the eight terrible cremation grounds.
Or one should contemplate [it] as having a radiance equal to the color red— meaning it is both red and red-radiant.

"By the mind" means by the drop (*bindu*) of the perfectly pure mind called "Hero," which, having vibrated while residing in the pericarp, is perceived as abiding in the four petals of the directions.

"Joined with the four goddesses" means that when there is an emanation from the drops (*bindu*) at the eastern petal and so forth, respectively, of the infinite members of the families (*kula*) of Vajra, Maṇi, Padma, and Karma, as well as their *Utkulas*, [the central deity] is seated upon those very petals by means of Vajra-Ḍākinī, Ratna-Ḍākinī, Padma-Ḍākinī, and Viśva-Ḍākinī, who are produced through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). || 7 ||
"Adorned with the image of the Buddha":
the Buddha is Vajradhara;
his image, that is, his form, is Śrī Heruka.

It is adorned by that leader of the maṇḍala. It is further adorned by the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, who is embraced by those very goddesses; he has emerged from the transformation of the two seed-syllables—which were impelled by the songs to be described from the root *manobindu*—and he pervades the directions with the radiance of the five family-lords (*pañcakuleśa*). He is manifested through the dissolution and resurgence of those [rays] via the transformation of the two seed-syllables.
Regarding the nature of that Buddha-image, he says "pūrva" and so forth.
"Four-faced" means having four mouths.
"Four-armed and three-eyed" is easy to understand.
In the north, one should meditate upon [the deity] who is red in color, surrounded by garlands of flames,
three-eyed, beautiful, four-faced, and four-armed.
One should visualize the goddess with three eyes in the east; in her left hands, a khaṭvāṅga and a bell, and likewise in her right hands, a vajra and a skull-cup.
In the goddess’s right [hands], there is a trident, a jewel, a banner, and a jackal;
in the goddess’s left [hands], there is a bow, an arrow, a double-lotus, and a skull-cup.
In the upper left hand of the goddess are a sword, a noose, a hand-drum, and a skull-cup. || 10 ||
He states what color each face has: the eastern face is the color of a blue lotus, the southern face is yellow,
and the western face is white.
The meaning is that it is red-colored on the northern face;
and it is well known that whatever color is at the root and on the face, that same [color] is on the body.
Regarding the phrase *jvālāmālākulam*: it is so described because it is crowded with garlands (*mālā*) of flames (*jvālā*) equal to the fire of universal destruction (*pralayānala*). || 8-9 ||

With the words beginning with "on the left" (vāme), he describes the emblems of the goddesses: "she who has a khaṭvāṅga and a bell on the left" means she whose left [hands] hold a khaṭvāṅga and a bell;
"likewise, with a vajra and a skull-cup in her right hands" means she who has a vajra and a skull-cup in her two right hands.
"In the east" means on the eastern petal.
"The Goddess"—
this term is to be connected everywhere in all subsequent instances as well.
Here, first, is Vajraḍākinī;
subsequently, in due order, Ratnaḍākinī, Padmaḍākinī, and Viśvaḍākinī.
"In the south," and so forth.
"She who has a trident, a jewel, a banner, and a jackal in her hand" is how she is described.
Regarding the word "paścimena" (in the west):
the instrumental case is used here in the sense of the locative.
The bow, the arrow, the universal lotus, and the skull; by virtue of possessing these, she is "the one who holds the bow, arrow, universal lotus, and skull" (dhanurbāṇaviśvapadmakapālinī).
Regarding the phrase "with a sword," and so forth:
The sword, the noose, the hand-drum, and the skull-cup—these are the vajras of body, speech, and mind; one should contemplate them there in the center.
Furthermore, [he holds] the skull-cup and the khaṭvāṅga, as well as the bow and the arrow. (11)
Having meditated upon it as conjoined with the initial mantra, it blazes up at that very moment;
likewise, the yogi accomplishes the substance that bestows the fruit of siddhi. 12.
She is so called because these [shaktis] are in her hands;
they too are garlanded with flames, four-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed,
for qualities follow the nature of their principal.
Therefore, according to the direction of the Blessed One’s face, the eastern [face] is blue in color, the southern is yellow,
and the western is white in color.
The northern one is dark-complexioned;
their faces are likewise, but the color of their bodies is the same as that of their root-faces.
In place of their body-colored faces, O Blessed One, their faces have become blue. ||10||
He describes the signs of the Blessed One’s abode with the words beginning with "body":
Śrī Heruka is the vajra of body, speech, and mind;
one should meditate upon him.
" therein " means in the red lotus;
" in the center " means in the pericarp (*karṇikā*);
"the skull," and so forth.
The phrase "in his hands" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Just as Śrī Heruka is, so too is Buddhadākinī; however, she is red in color and has a red principal face.
And she appeared before him, her neck firmly embraced by his two arms. ||11||
Without the *samaya*, there are no accomplishments (*siddhi*);
therefore, he says "beginning with *ādi*" and so forth in order to explain the kindling of the *samaya*.
The connection is that the *samaya* substance, when conjoined with the *ādimantra*—which is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*)—blazes forth.
"Having meditated" means when one has meditated according to the instruction.
"Substance" refers to the substance of the pledge (*samayadravya*).
"Accomplishes" means he brings it to completion.
What does it accomplish?
It bestows the fruit of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
And it is said in the glorious *Guhyasamāja*: "Having meditated upon the syllable *Oṃ* of all mantras, it blazes forth at that very moment" (16.38). ||12||
Through yoga and perfected yoga, confidence arises instantaneously;
by means of internal restraint, he becomes invisible, illuminating the entire thousandfold world-system. ||13||
He captivates all the siddhas and enjoys the celestial maidens;
he perceives Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, abiding within the vajra-lattice. (14)

With the vajra-eye, he perceives as many realms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, along with the characteristics of body, speech, and mind, as clearly as an amalaka fruit in his own hand. (15)
For they cultivate the drama called "mind," which abides as the self of all, perfected by the unsurpassed reality, established in the awakening of the Buddhas, and auspicious. (16)
He states the praise of the flames with the words "The yogas," and so forth.
Here, the yogas are indeed the yogis themselves.
The conviction arises in the world that there exist yogis and yoginīs who have attained accomplishment (*siddha*).
The meaning is: "because of seeing the blazing of the illustration of power.
He describes the power consisting of the accomplishment of invisibility and so forth with the words beginning with "antah" (within). [He says: "the illuminator of a single thousandfold world-system."
A thousand world-systems consisting of four continents is a small chiliocosm; he illuminates each one of these through his sovereignty and his performance of the welfare of others. ||13||
"Of all the siddhas" refers to the vidyādharas and others;
"a maiden" is to be supplied [as the object].
The vajra-abode is the established buddha-field of those very Buddhas.
This is their assembly;
"together with them" means those who are established in the vajra-abode. (14)
The "vajra-eye" is the eye-vajra;
it means the supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) of the two eyes.
"In one's own hand," and so forth.
The meaning is: "just as a single *āmalaka* fruit held in one's own hand.
Here, the seals (*mudrā*) in the form of verses for body, speech, and mind are the marks of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Substances, meditations, and contemplations,
as well as various kinds of means, have been demonstrated and taught as desired by the Goddess. ||17||
Regarding the characteristic of mind: bodily and mental [states] are the sensory consciousnesses;
vocal and mental [states] are the mental consciousnesses.
Because they involve discursive speech;
their characteristic is their essential nature,
and "they cultivate" means they perceive them with the mind.
How do they see? "As the self of all," meaning as the universal self.
To the question "What is this?", he says: "The mind," and so forth.
"Citta-khyā" means the vajra-mind;
it signifies the knowledge of the minds of others.
In Yoga Tantra, the meditation on oneself in the form of one's own deity is the "nāṭaka" (drama) here.
Because it is associated with drama (*nāṭaka*).
Therefore, its origin is from this.
As it has been stated: "In the procurement of the ritual substances and materials, only a small amount was mentioned."
Since even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess such auspiciousness as this, he distinguishes [the Buddha's state] by saying "that reality" (tattva).
The meaning is that it is knowledge free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Such knowledge also exists for Bodhisattvas, but it is surpassed by the knowledge of a Buddha.
Then, for the sake of further specification, he says: "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
It is called "unsurpassed" because there is nothing superior to it. ||15-16||
Regarding the phrase "here, the verse":
this is a summary verse concerning the meaning of the Tantra as it has been explained.
"Forms" refers to the colors and configurations of the deities and so forth.
"Mudrāṇi" means "mudrās. These are the six limbs, such as the purification of the vajra and lotus, which are the very symbols of that [deity].
In whosever house this tantra may always exist— whether one upholds it, recites it, or meditates upon it—
therein there shall be no disease, no old age, and no death.
The goddesses protect against obstacles. ||18||
Thus concludes the great secret of the Mahāvajra-Ḍākinīs, together with its ritual procedures. This is the third instruction.
Thus ends the Mahāmāyā Tantra.
The skull-bowl, the khaṭvāṅga staff, and so forth;
these are the substances, the objects of the pledge (samaya).
As for "meditations":
The root *dhyai* means "to contemplate";
the meaning here is "repetitions" (*japāḥ*).
"Meditative realizations" (*bhāvanāni*) refers to the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the maṇḍala, the wheel (*cakra*), and so forth.

Various means, such as the lack of success in the expansion of karma and so forth—these have all been demonstrated and indicated. To the question, "What has been accomplished by all of this? he says: "The Goddess," and so on.
Those things which were desired by the mind and longed for in the heart by the Goddess Mahāmāyā have been spoken. ||17||
He states the benefit of embracing the *tantra* with the verse beginning with "the *tantra*," etc.
"The *tantra*" refers to that called *Mahāmāyā*.
"In whose house" means in the house of whichever person.
"Bhaveta nityam" means it remains eternally;
"dhāreta" means one should maintain it;
"vāceta" means one should cause it to be recited.
The meaning is "one should recite.
"Vibhāvayeta" means "one should contemplate.
"Vighnāni" means "obstacles. ||18||
And those [deities] are the great Vajra-Ḍākinīs;
their "mata" (mata) means the accepted doctrine or established tenet, which signifies the entire Yoginī-tantra.
Its secret is its essence.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The great secret.
At the beginning, it was called the "supreme secret."
The meaning is that what was previously stated as "that very great secret" is here expressed by another synonym, namely, the tantra called *Mahāmāyā*.
That [tantra] is completed and finalized.
It is "with its ritual services."
The term *vidhi* (prescription) refers to the meaning of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*); that which exists together with this is *sopacāra*,
meaning it is not devoid of that.
Whatever merit has been acquired by me through this commentary on the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*, which is like the radiance of the full moon, may it be transformed [for the benefit of all].

May I become the singular self of the Victors, possessing the nature of the Vajra-Holder; through that, may there be the ultimate exhaustion of suffering for me, and may the entire world attain it as well.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*.
The *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*,
composed by the great paṇḍita Ratnākaraśānti, is hereby completed.
That which is neither one nor many, the foundation of the great perfection that benefits both self and others,
neither non-existence nor existence, whose nature is as difficult to discern as it is like one's own self,
equal in flavor, stainless, changeless, auspicious, peerless, all-pervading, and free from conceptual proliferation; [that is the Self].
I pay homage to that incomparable Dharmakāya of the Victors, which is to be personally realized within.
The *Mahāmāyāsādhana*:
the deity named Mahāmāyā, who has four faces and four arms,
with the Goddess likewise upon his lap, and four others in the [four] directions.
Out of compassion for Mahāvajradhara himself, who possesses a terrifying form,
the sādhana of the one known as Mahāmāyā is now properly explained.

In this regard, the practitioner (mantrin) authorized for the stage of cultivation, awakened by the exhortation of the songs of the four goddesses, should rise at dawn. Having purified himself with rays from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the sun within his own heart, and having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, he should effect the protection of the site and the self with the mantra *HŪṂ PHAṬ*. Then, entering the meditation chamber and consecrating the water offering (*arghya*) with the syllable *HŪṂ*, he sits upon a comfortable seat. Visualizing the Blessed One together with his retinue in the space before him, he should worship them with clouds of the five offerings arising from the rays of the heart-mantra. He should then perform the confession of sins and so forth, as follows: "I confess my own sin."
I rejoice in all merits;
I dedicate all my own roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
until awakening, I go for refuge to the Three Jewels.
The jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha— oh,

may I indeed attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings, in order to establish them in ultimate, final nirvāṇa and in the unsurpassed knowledge of a Tathāgata.

Thereafter, one should resolve that all this is mind-only (*cittamātra*), appearing in various unreal forms just as in a dream; having abandoned all [conceptual] forms, one should perceive the infinite, mere luminosity, which is like the stainless sky and free from appearances, and should consecrate oneself with the thought: "I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness (*śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāva*). *Oṃ*.

Immediately thereafter, having visualized a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) by means of the syllable *hūṃ* in the sun in the space before one, and through the radiating flashes of its blazing rays, one should contemplate the ground below as consisting of vajras, the vajra-fence across the sides, the vajra-canopy above, and in the center, a formidable cremation ground; then, in the middle of that, one should see a single-chambered gabled temple (*kūṭāgāra*) made of all kinds of jewels—
quadrangular, with four doors, and adorned with four archways.
And with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as apsarases, there were four radiant altars.

Having meditated upon an eight-petalled red lotus in the center of that, one should meditate on the drop of the nectar of gnosis—which is without beginning or end and resembles a pearl of the *tāra* syllable—within its pericarp.
This is the first samādhi, called the "Beginningless Yoga.
From that very central drop, one should visualize four drops radiating out to the petals in the eight directions, seeing them transformed into the form of seed-syllables.
In sequence: *huṃ*, *svā*, *ā*, *hāḥ*.

Having sequentially emanated from them the lords of the Vajra, Jewel, Lotus, and Action families, along with their respective families, and having again withdrawn them back into those very [syllables], one should visualize the four Yoginīs transformed from them:
on the eastern petal, Vajraḍākinī, blue in color, with faces that are blue, yellow, white, and green, holding a vajra, a skull-cup, a bell, and a khaṭvāṅga.
On the southern petal is Ratnaḍākinī, yellow in color, with faces that are yellow, blue, white, and green; she holds a stream of jewels, a trident, a garland of skulls, and a banner of a jackal.
On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white in color, with faces that are white, yellow, blue, and green; she holds a universal lotus, an arrow, a skull-cup, and a bow.
On the northern petal is Viśvaḍākinī, green in color, with faces that are green, yellow, white, and blue; she holds a sword, a *ḍamaru* drum, a noose, and a skull-cup.
All [the goddesses] possess the radiance of moon-seats.
They should awaken him—their lord and master, like Śeṣa—for the remaining months, with this vajra-song: "O friend! Behold, the lotus has been awakened by the thunderbolt!"
"Alalalalaho! Come, let us dance with great joy! he cried.
By the sun's rays, the lotus blossomed with great joy;
with "alalalalaho," he danced with great joy.
Then, by the power of the song, the Blessed One, having abandoned the form of the drop (bindu), manifests in the form of two seed-syllables: OṂ HŪṂ.
Then, having emanated Vairocana and his family from the syllable *oṃ*, one should reabsorb them; likewise, from the syllable *hūṃ*, one emanates the five Jinas and their families.
Then, together with the Buddha-Ḍākinī arisen from the syllable *oṃ*, the Blessed Lord Heruka arises from the syllable *hūṃ*.
Smeared with ashes, Kṛṣṇa possesses a splendor like that of the seat of the lovely sun;
his tawny hair blazes upward, and he is formidable with a crown of skulls.
He has four faces— blue, yellow, great white, and green—
and eight arms, holding a skull-cup, an arrow, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a bow.
Through the purification of the five Buddhas, he is adorned with the five mudrās:
the wheel, the earrings, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle.
Clad in human skin, with twelve reddish eyes,
his wrath filled with garlands of flames, yet beautiful with supreme bliss.
Standing in the half-lotus dance posture and endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments,
he accomplishes the welfare of the world through the multitudes of beings projected from his inner organ.
Śrī Buddhaḍākinī has faces that are red, yellow, white, and green; she is fond of her consort’s weapons, is red in color, and has both arms embracing his neck.
Just as the Śabarī initiation of the Buddha is sung in the Hevajra [tantra],
so here Heruka is fully worshipped by the Buddha-Ḍākinī.
The Buddha is "red" here because he delights sentient beings with his Buddha-body;
the dharmas are pure by nature—this is the whiteness of the Lord of Speech.

Thereafter, one should contemplate a red syllable *ūṃ* at the Blessed One’s faculty of sight, a blue *huṃ* at the faculty of hearing, a yellow *cīṃ* at the faculty of smell, a white *āḥ* at the faculty of taste, a green *repha* at the location of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and a white *kha* in the mind. This is the placement of the six syllables upon the six faculties.
The armor: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*—this is the consecration of body, speech, and mind, applied respectively to the head, throat, and heart.

Having visualized the seed-syllable of one's own deity, whose nature is that gnosis, upon a sun disk between the breasts, one should summon the gnosis-maṇḍala with the hooks of its rays; having expelled the obstacles with the syllable *hūṃ*, offered the water for honor (*arghya*), and [uttered] *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, one should see the pledge-maṇḍala (*samaya-maṇḍala*) as having become one with it through being summoned, made to enter, bound, and brought under control.

Then, impelled by the rays from the seed-syllable of gnosis, five yoginīs sent by the Tathāgatas arrive; they, along with the Blessed Ones, should consecrate [the practitioner] with precious vases filled with the water of the five gnoses.
As they are being consecrated, the Lord of their own family arises upon their heads. Thus the Blessed One spoke regarding the sprinkling.
The [Buddhas] corresponding to the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and the others are, in order, Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Vāgīśa, and Amoghasiddhi.

Then, one should worship the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady with the five offerings and the worship of the five qualities of sensual pleasure, emanated from the rays issuing from the faces of the seed-syllables of gnosis (*jñānabīja*).
Thereafter, one should praise the Blessed Lord through the mouths of the goddesses:
"I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is adorned with a garland of severed heads and terrifying fangs, and who is devouring great flesh. Then,
through the yoga of radiating light, the goddesses of the directions should dissolve into Buddha-Ḍākinī.

Then, having visualized the syllables *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *svā*, *ā*, and *hā* in her head, heart, navel, secret place, and thighs respectively, and having pervaded her body with these [syllables] flashing from one limit to another,

he should begin the passion (*rati*) and attachment (*anurāga*)— using the mantra "I go" (*yāmi*)— with her red lotus born from the syllable *hrīḥ* and its pearl pericarp born from the syllable *a*, and with his vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* and its jewel born from the syllable *oṃ*.
Then, the Tathāgatas, impelled by the rays of light from the two jewels, arrive, enter through the mouth, dissolve, and fall upon the petals of the lotus.
One should contemplate that fivefold nectar of wisdom being taken up with a graceful movement of the tip of the tongue.
This is the second meditative absorption, named Śrīmaṇḍalarājāgri.

Then, impelled by the Blessed One, the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and others, through the radiations of clouds of the bodies of the five Blessed Ones, act for the benefit of sentient beings in due order: the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the perfectly pure wisdom of the dharma-realm (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).

Having generated the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), and the state of the Great Vajradhara, they should dissolve their own clouds of bodies into the root body.
This is the third meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Awakened by Karma.
Furthermore, if the yogi should wish to stabilize the mind:

For the sake of accomplishing the foremost of all siddhis, one should then briefly contemplate the three samādhis: having meditated upon the navel-lotus pericarp as being without seams at the edges of the union of the sun and moon, one should visualize within it a hero consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), in the form of a drop (*bindu*) that is subtle like a mustard seed, white, transparent, and the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*). Then, one should contemplate a ray of light, resembling a lotus fiber, which emerges through the center of the moon and remains encircling the union with three coils.
Having seen [the moon], one should visualize sixteen syllables each, strung together within the three half-coils situated upon the moon.
For it is said in the *Saṃvarottara*: "One should arrange the letters from *ka* to *da*, excluding *ṅ* and *ña*."
"One should draw two lines beginning with the letter *dh* and ending with the letter *ā*;
the line of the letter *a* should be placed in the center upon the lunar disc. Thus it is said.
Here too, it is stated: "by means of divine rows of syllables" (1.26).

Thus, meditating on the Hero within the interior of the union of the sun and moon at the pericarp of the lotus in the center of the navel, and being intent upon the maturation of that meditation, one should perceive [the Hero] as situated from that very place like a single flame blazing from a second subtle line.
By its power...
The hero, flooded by a surging stream of flowing nectar, and that line of rays shall become white.
Then, with his mind restrained upon the hero, he should gaze at him until, through the signs, he perceives the attainment of stability of mind.

When stability has been observed, one should contemplate that line of rays as clearly illuminating the infinite universe; then, seeing everything like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, one will quickly accomplish all meditative absorptions (*samādhis*).
This is the *binduyoga*.

The accomplishment of one who has recited the vidyā is called *japa*. In the same way, the yogin, having meditated for a long time upon the wheel of the six deities situated within the cavity of the union of the sun and moon located in the pericarp of the navel-lotus, should likewise recite the mantra with the three rows of syllables strung together by a line of its rays, joined with the three enclosures.
In this tantra, the mantras consist of three syllables.
Among them, the mantra of the Blessed One is: oṃ hūṃ hūṃ.
The seed syllables for the Buddha-Ḍākinīs and the others, in their respective order, are: ŪṂ ŪṂ HŪṂ,
ŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ,
ŪṂ SVĀ HŪṂ, ŪṂ Ā HŪṂ, ŪṂ HĀ HŪṂ.
How should one recite?

Having placed the seed-syllable to be recited within the interior of the *saṃpuṭa*, and having raised the Hero (*vīra*) above its head while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, one should raise a line of light-rays from the Hero with the exhalation breath and, illuminating [the world] with that, make the universe consist of the Buddha.

While reciting the seed-syllable, one should resolve that all those Buddhas have the nature of one's own deity. Reciting the syllable *HŪṂ* within, one should draw in that world consisting of Buddhas by means of the breath of exhalation and dissolve it into the Hero (*vīra*).
One should perform this again and again.
This should be done until weariness arises.

When weariness occurs, one should rest; then, having dedicated all this merit toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and the attainment of the desired fruit, and having performed worship as before, one should arise from the seed-syllable at one's own heart, resolve that oneself is of the nature of one's chosen deity, and perform everything [else].

Having transformed all food into the nectar of the five gnoses by means of the five seed-syllables, and having visualized and meditated upon the circle of deities within one’s own heart, one should offer that nectar into their tongues.
While bathing, one should contemplate the ritual of the consecration of the deities.

At the midday and evening junctions (saṃdhyā), however, having entered the maṇḍala house, one should emanate the foundational maṇḍala through rays of light from the seed-syllable in one’s heart; from that very seed-syllable, one should gradually manifest the four yoginīs.

Having seated [the deities] in their respective places and performed all the rites such as the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as before, one should dissolve the maṇḍala and then arise; thereafter, one should practice the yoga of meditative absorption (*samāhitayoga*) as previously described.

However, at the twilight of midnight, there is this distinction: having performed worship and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should dismiss the *jñānamaṇḍala* with the mantra "Oṃ Vajra Mur," dissolve the *samayamaṇḍala* into one's own *jñānabīja*, resolve upon the non-manifest bodhicitta, and go to sleep.
In this manner, on subsequent days as well, one should perform everything as before, impelled by the goddess’s exhortation to sing.
Thus, every day, until one obtains the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*).
In that regard, the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala is perfected through one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*).
For the remaining [deities], it is by ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-jāpa*).
The *mālā-mantras* are to be obtained from other tantras.

Having formed them into a circle as appropriate—either upon the sun at one's own heart or upon the moon at the heart—and having visualized them with the mind as blazing like a row of lamps, one should recite them mentally as if reading aloud.
By whatever merit I have acquired through thus speaking this *mahāmāyā-sādhana*,
may I become a Buddha, a master in accomplishing the welfare of all beings.
The *Mahāmāyāsādhana* is completed.
The Ritual Manual for the Sadhana of Mahāmāyā by Kukkurīpāda.
Homage to Vajraḍāka!

First, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated upon a soft cushion, one should visualize the seed-syllable *HŪṂ* within a solar disc at one’s own heart. Then, having meditated upon Karuṇācalavajra before oneself—possessing the colors, arms, and weapons to be described hereafter—and having performed the worship, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication of merit, going for refuge, and so forth, as well as the aspiration prayers, one should contemplate the name-syllable within one’s own body, speech, and mind.
And that name-syllable is: *He*, meaning "all phenomena are devoid of causes."
*Ha*: all phenomena are unproduced;
*e*: all phenomena are free from seeking;
*ru*: all phenomena are like an echo.
*Ra* means that all phenomena are endowed with delight;
*u* means that all phenomena are subject to the nature of arising and ceasing;
*ka* means that all phenomena are endowed with all happiness.
"A" is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen.
Having understood this and meditated upon emptiness, one should recite the mantra: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness*.

Having dispelled obstacles with the syllable *Hūṃ* and visualized a vajra-fence, one sees the seed-syllable *Hūṃ* within a solar mandala at the center of a red four-petaled lotus in the midst of the eight cremation grounds. [One then visualizes] the four goddesses whose natures are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

In the internal sādhana, they urge [the practitioner] with the glorious Vajra-song: "O friend! This lotus has been awakened by the syllable VAJREṂ. With great bliss, it has ascended while dancing in the manner of *alalalalaho*."
By the sun’s rays, the lotus has blossomed with great joy;
Alalalalaha has ascended to dance with great affection.
"By means of the dance of the Vajraḍākinīs, one should establish Vajrasattva.

Immediately following this song, through the mental realization of phenomena as being bound by illusion, one should visualize Karuṇācalavajra, arisen from the syllable *HŪṂ*. He has four faces—blue, yellow, white, and dark—and four arms.

In his right hands he holds a skull-cup and an arrow; in his left, he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff and a bow. He stands in a wrathful posture (*raudrāsana*), possesses three eyes, wears a garland of fresh severed heads, and is adorned on his head with a string of skulls. He is further embellished with ornaments of bone.

His face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and his tawny hair stands erect. Upon his body is the yellow syllable *CĪ*; in the eyes is the white syllable *ŪM*; in the ears is the red syllable *HŪM*; in the nose is the white syllable *KHA*;

in the throat is the white syllable *ĀḤ*; and in the heart is the syllable *RE*. He is characterized by the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), embraced by the Wisdom Consort who is his own reflection, pervading the expanse of space, and [is consecrated] by Vajradhara.

Having visualized oneself as the *kīla* empowered by body, speech, and mind, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*, [one should meditate on] Vajraḍākinī on the eastern petal. She is blue in color, with four faces—blue, yellow, red, and dark green—and four arms. In her left hands she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* and a bell; in her right hands she holds a vajra and a skull-cup. Her intrinsic nature is that of the earth element and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

On the southern petal is Ratnaḍākinī, yellow in color, with four faces—yellow, blue, red, and dark green—and four arms; she holds a banner and a bodice in her left hands, and a trident and a jewel in her right hands, and her nature is the wisdom of the equality of the water element. On the western petal is Padmaḍākinī, white and reddish in color, with four faces—red, yellow, blue, and dark green—and four arms; she holds a bow and a skull-cup in her left hands, and an arrow and a double-lotus in her right hands, and her nature is the wisdom of discernment of the fire element.

On the northern petal is Viśvaḍākinī, dark green in color, with four faces—dark green, yellow, red, and blue—and four arms. In her left hands she holds a noose and a skull-cup; in her right hands she holds a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaru drum. Her nature is the performance of the activity of the wind element.

All these goddesses stand upon fierce seats, their heads adorned with garlands of skulls, wearing necklaces of strings of fresh severed heads, possessing three eyes, with faces made terrifying by slightly bared fangs, and with flaming, upright, tawny hair. They are encircled by a blazing garland of rays.

Having thus meditated upon oneself as Karuṇācalavajra surrounded by the four goddesses, and having visualized, according to the oral instruction, the maṇḍalas of Vāyu, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and Agni at the head, heart, navel, and secret place, the practitioner of mantra should perform the neuter recitation (*napuṃsakajāpa*).

When weary, having performed the mantra recitation with *oṃ āḥ hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ*, the yogi— whose nature is the Dharma established in the mantra that is the essence of all phenomena equal to cyclic existence (*bhava*)— should perform all activities such as the sense objects for the sake of liberation from ordinary conceptualization.
Thus ends the *Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā*.
This is the work of Kukkuri-pāda.
